sourceSpan.excerpt: In contrast, there's what I've called the the physicist sense of fine-tuned. In this sense of fine-tuning, it's not the universe that we're thinking about, but rather a theory is supposed to be a feature that a theory can have. And a theory has that feature when its free parameters have unnatural or improbable values. So down below we have this uh this passage from Luke Barnes. So he puts it the uh the point this way. So we're thinking about the probability of some data d given some theory t and uh in background knowledge b. He's saying that this likelihood is much less than one. And then he says that this is what a physicist means by fine-tune. Right? So don't take just my word for it that this is a uh one thing a physicist might mean by fine-tuning. This is what Luke Barnes, one of the proponents of the fine-tuning argument, says physicists mean by fine-tuning. Then he tells us that it's a special case of Beijian theory testing that fine-tuned or unnatural theories have very small likelihoods. And the more fine-tuned, the smaller the likelihood. Now, a small likelihood is not a sufficient reason to discard a theory. Rather, it presents an explainable but as yet unexplained fact. So, a good reason to examine our background assumptions and or search for an alternative theory. Perhaps one whose free parameters are not as fine-tuned or in the quantity alpha, that's your free parameter, is not a free parameter at all.
